new_statements.second_reader_evidence: byte-identical to cowl1242/; Acrobat scanned text layer, 15 two-up sheets = printed pp. 175-204, odd page left / even page right; rendered sheets 5 and 12 to PNG to confirm). Quote 1 is verbatim at p. 183 (sheet 5, left column, sec. 12, right after examples (18)): "This reduplication looks at first like simple -C2 reduplication because stress most commonly falls on the first vowel of the root; however, enough examples like 'he is going home slowly' occur to indicate that it is location of stress, and not root shape, that determines what is repeated." (text layer: "rool shape, Ihal delermines", as the report notes). Quote 2 is verbatim but at p. 197, not p. 193: sheet 12 left column carries…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary (high) stress per word (Kinkade 1963 sec. 1.1.2, fragments: 'Every noun and verb occurs with one and only one high stress'); its position is morphologically governed rather than phonologically predictable: most commonly on the first vowel of the root, but an affix may carry the high stress, in which case the stem is reduced to low (or secondary) stress and a root schwa deletes or becomes a; Rowicka 2002:143 (open, saved): 'stress generally tends to be restricted to lexical morphemes', with word-final one-consonant grammatical suffixes (-m, -c, -n) drawing stress onto a schwa before them; Kinkade 1998 (fragments) suggests stress is assigned to a morpheme rather than to a vowel or syllable. No weight or syllable-count rule is stated anywhere.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Kinkade 1963 sec. 1.1.2 (fragments) posits three stress phonemes, high (primary), secondary and low: 'Compound and reduplicated stems frequently have a high and a secondary stress, but the order in which they occur is variable. Secondary stress is not as common as high stress.' Rowicka 2000:114 treats Upper Chehalis as a language where 'only primary stress is manifested' (no secondary stresses). HNAI 7 key: v (low), v (high), v (secondary).
new_statements.exceptions: Particles mostly carry low stress, a few have high or secondary stress, and some low-stressed particles take high stress inside compounds (Kinkade 1963 fragments); stress shifts from root to certain suffixes (a causative-related suffix 'is always stressed', Kinkade 1993:191; slow-reduplication -aC forms always stressed on the suffix, Kinkade 1985:190); Rowicka 2002 notes the stress system has not been exhaustively analysed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (noun/verb words; particles behave differently); compounds form one phonological unit with a single primary stress (Kinkade 1993:193). Kinkade 1963 sec. 1.8.1 describes the phonetic exponent as pitch change plus amplitude, entangled with juncture/intonation. Rowicka's data are dictionary citation forms from Kinkade 1991.
new_statements.identity_note: Language-level uppe1439. Kinkade's Upper Chehalis data (the basis of every source here, including Rowicka's) come chiefly from the Oakville Chehalis dialect (his main consultant Silas Heck; Boas's 'Upper Chehalis 1'); the Satsop and Tenino Chehalis dialects are poorly attested. No separate dialect glottocodes were checked.

sources.note: p. 143: 'Although an exhaustive analysis of the Upper Chehalis stress system still needs to be carried out, stress generally tends to be restricted to lexical morphemes.' Stress on a weak root's schwa rather than a following full-vowel grammatical suffix (7a), but word-final monoconsonantal suffixes -m, -c, -n draw stress onto the schwa before them (7b), (10) p. 146; fn 10 stressed schwa ~ unstressed a root alternation is regular (Kinkade 1998). Data from Kinkade 1991.
